title: The Critical Risk Hiding Across Your Technology Estate: End of Support Dates
summary: Learn why end-of-support & end-of-life dates for enterprise technology pose major risks for organizations & get expert advice on assessing risk exposure.
body_markdown:
Across an organization’s enterprise technology estate, a support deadline, a vendor change or the loss of specialist knowledge can turn a dependable system into an urgent business decision.


As Chief Client Officer, I spend a great deal of time listening to clients share their technology challenges and priorities. What I’ve found is that IT leaders want both: to keep the business running and to retain the freedom to decide what happens next and they are always looking for ways to find incremental and immediate savings to fund new projects.


The conversation often starts with a renewal or a support deadline which opens up a strategic discussion about their overall technology roadmap. Organizations need a clear plan either to support the technology after vendor support ends or to move to a replacement platform, which could take months of rebuilding integrations, testing and retraining – not to mention the budget implications. Without that preparation, a single support deadline could force IT teams into rushed decisions that derail the wider roadmap and budget.


The impending retirement of on-premises UKG Workforce Central, formerly Kronos Workforce Central, illustrates the broader risk of business disruption. End of life is[scheduled for March 31, 2027](https://www.healthcareitleaders.com/blog/ukg-workforce-central-wfc-end-of-life/) . A workforce management application may never appear on a board agenda. But when employees can’t access their schedules or time records, the operational disruption is unavoidable.


## What is the hidden technology risk?


We saw that tension firsthand when Broadcom’s acquisition of VMware changed the economics of virtualization.[Lwart Environmental Solutions](https://www.riministreet.com/clients/lwart-environmental-solutions/) faced a licensing model that would have tripled its costs.[Alcatel-Lucent Enterprise](https://www.riministreet.com/clients/alcatel-lucent-enterprise/) (ALE) also faced a choice between a sharp increase or a hasty migration. Their situation warns of a broader issue that CIOs need to address.


This event shows how reliance on a technology can become a financial and operational pressure point, a risk that grows if IT leaders can’t clearly see which systems depend on it, when support or other lifecycle changes are approaching or where support is missing.


End-of-support dates, vendor mergers and acquisitions, renewals and the loss of specialist knowledge are triggers. The consequences can include downtime, unexpected costs, compliance exposure and emergency migration costs. **The loss of control over a business-critical system often pushes IT and finance teams into an urgent, expensive decision on someone else’s timeline.**


## Finding application risks before they find you


Application risks rarely develop overnight. They build as new integrations increase dependencies, support responsibilities become fragmented and specialist knowledge becomes concentrated in fewer hands. Each change may seem manageable on its own, but together they can leave the business more exposed to disruption when vendor roadmaps or industry conditions shift.


The major ERP platforms rightly receive executive attention. Yet many other peripheral applications, databases and infrastructure that run the business rarely receive the same scrutiny.[MuleSoft’s 2025 Connectivity Benchmark research](https://www.salesforce.com/blog/mulesoft-connectivity-benchmark-2025/) found that enterprises manage an average of 897 applications, with nearly a third of them integrated with other applications. That scale makes it difficult to see every dependency. Often, by the time an application becomes an executive priority, the time needed to evaluate alternatives, test changes and protect continuity may already be gone.


> “Enterprises manage an average of 897 applications, with nearly a third of them integrated with other applications.” – 2025 MuleSoft Connectivity Benchmark Report


## How to assess your risk exposure


Use these five questions as a practical starting point for understanding areas of exposure and evaluating your application risk:


1. **Operational dependency:** *Which enterprise software and platforms could interrupt a critical process if they failed tomorrow?*
A small component can sit on a critical path. Map each technology to the business services and systems that depend on it, including interfaces and manual workarounds. Confirm acceptable downtime and test the workarounds so priorities reflect operational consequences rather than visibility.
2. **Support complexity:** *Are support ownership and escalation responsibilities fragmented?*
Different vendors, contracts and escalation routes can leave teams debating ownership while an incident continues. Review who leads when an issue crosses application, database and infrastructure boundaries. Assign an accountable owner and agree on escalation paths before an outage.
3. **Lifecycle pressure:** *Which lifecycle events could force a rushed decision in the next 12–24 months?*
Support retirements, renewals and vendor changes can compress decision windows when preparation starts too late. Bring these events into one view and work backward from the time needed to assess alternatives, address security and compliance requirements, test integrations and execute a transition. A renewal date alone is not a plan.
4. **Concentrated expertise:** *Where does continuity depend on a few specialists or undocumented knowledge?*
A critical technology may be entirely reliant on a single individual’s knowledge of its customizations, interfaces and recovery procedures. Document the information and processes, establish backup capability and test recovery with someone other than the usual expert. This turns individual knowledge into organizational readiness.
5. **Business criticality:** *Which systems should remain stable while the organization invests elsewhere?*
Evaluate the consequence of failure, not simply usage or spend. A monthly payroll interface may matter more at a particular moment than a widely used reporting tool. Use that business impact to identify where continued support and targeted optimization can protect critical operations, and where security, compliance or capability gaps necessitate change.


By building visibility into dependencies and support gaps, you can address the most consequential risks first and establish viable options to maintain, optimize, replace or retire systems on a business-led timeline.

ALE gained support for its existing environment while retaining room to evaluate its virtualization strategy. Lwart continued operating its VMware investment without accepting the proposed tripling of costs.


“Either we would need to absorb a massive increase in licensing costs with Broadcom or pursue alternate paths,” said Jefferson Andriotti, Head of IT and Procurement at Lwart. “We looked at moving to Nutanix or Citrix, but because Rimini Street had done so well with our SAP support, we thought, why not use them for VMware, too?”

We take the proven expertise in exceptional support that clients have trusted for decades to keep their most complex systems running and apply it to these at-risk applications, bringing the same tried-and-tested approach to more of the technology estate. The aim is to address support gaps across the environment and provide more comprehensive support. That work follows three priorities:

- **Prioritize the response:** Assess business impact to determine where continued support can protect stability and where change is a priority.
- **Create choice:** Explore options suited to the complexity of your environment to ensure flexibility before circumstances force the decision.


Working with a single, proven provider that supports more of your technologies and whose expertise covers customizations and integrations can reduce handoffs, simplify vendor management and clarify accountability. For IT leaders, fewer support distractions mean more capacity for AI and modernization with greater flexibility to handle unexpected changes without losing sight of business priorities – this is where their focus is.
